entries.title: Anita Brookner by Hermione Lee review – an enigmatic literary great given her due
entries.summary: This exhaustive biography of the Booker winner brings her properly out of the shadows for the first time‘Dr Weiss, at forty, knew that her life had been ruined by literature.” The first fictional sentence Anita Brookner ever published, aged 53, in A Start in Life, certainly set a tone. entries.content:
‘Dr Weiss, at forty, knew that her life had been ruined by literature.” The first fictional sentence Anita Brookner ever published, aged 53, in A Start in Life, certainly set a tone. If people have heard of Brookner today, Hermione Lee says, they imagine a lonely, cardiganed woman yearning for an absent lover. “This,” says Lee (an emeritus English professor at the University of Oxford), “won’t do.”

The cardiganed image confuses the author with her protagonists. Of 24 novels written across 30 years, only the first four – A Start in Life, Providence, Look at Me and Hotel du Lac – are about a single woman pining for love. There is certainly a “Brooknerian” style, characterised by elegance, restraint and melancholia, but her fiction engaged with our emotional lives broadly, examining family, exile, home, trauma, ageing and much more.

Born in 1928 and raised in south London by a fearsome Polish-Jewish grandmother and absurdly ineffectual parents (a tobacco salesman and a failed singer), Brookner was a highly academic only child. After a degree at King’s College London, she briefly tasted freedom as a student in Paris, but was soon dragged back to care for her extraordinarily needy mother. Yoked to home for the next decade, she managed, nevertheless, to become a brilliant art critic and a charismatic lecturer at the Courtauld Institute, where she stayed until retirement.

In the introduction, Lee describes hearing the author’s voice saying, repeatedly, “Go away”, and Brookner’s 20s and 30s were the “most hidden, the least witnessed” of all. Brookner did her utmost to erase her life, and Lee is forced, therefore, to mine any detail she can find. As well as Brookner’s academic work and extensive reading habits, we get her poor handwriting, fear of trains, love of perfumes and at one particularly desperate point, salary increases over two decades. A couple of love affairs in her 30s fizzled out, but if there was ever a record of her feelings, Brookner expunged it. The first 200 pages, then, can be hard going. She was, says Lee, through gritted teeth, “an object of mystery and puzzlement”.

But Lee persists – always rake thin, Brookner kept slimming biscuits in her handbag; she loved babies; she doled out tranquillisers to nervous PhD candidates – and just as this enterprise starts to feel doomed, something miraculous happens. The tireless details begin to cohere and Brookner steps out of the shadows, intriguing, contradictory – the super brain who shaved 10 years off her age in her own Who’s Who entry; the self-proclaimed “loneliest woman in London” who had loads of friends.

The older she gets, the more interesting this book becomes. In 1979, her beloved Courtauld mentor, friend and boss, Anthony Blunt, was exposed as a Soviet spy. Shaken, Brookner remained loyal until she discovered he’d used her to extract information from a hospitalised colleague.

Reeling and depressed, facing another lonely summer, she found herself writing fiction. Her process was extraordinary. Each novel took only three months from start to finish. She’d roam London forming sentences in her head, then simply write them down, at speed. Hilary Mantel, a fervent admirer, said Brookner arrived as a novelist perfectly formed, “as if she had hatched from a marbled egg”. She would repeat this process, annually, for more than two decades.

In 1984, her fourth novel, Hotel du Lac, about a woman who jilts her fiancee and retreats to a Swiss hotel, won the Booker prize. Pretty much everyone expected JG Ballard’s Empire of the Sun or Julian Barnes’s Flaubert’s Parrot to win. The misogyny was mind-bending. At the ceremony, Ballard hissed, “You stole my Booker.” Private Eye snarked about “Hotel du Lac of Interest” and a grim pattern of critical disdain was set. For the rest of Brookner’s writing life, critics would carp about “doily” novels and compare her to Mills & Boon. Profiles were invariably illustrated with sad spinsters holding cups of tea. It tormented her. But she kept on writing.

She was, personally, far from isolated. She had devoted friends, including the Virago publisher Carmen Callil and fellow writers such as Rosamond Lehmann or Julian Barnes, who offers loving memories here. He was so intimidated by her eloquence when they lunched that he’d feel himself inserting semicolons into his own speech.

Was she a literary genius? She once, brilliantly, described novel-writing as “trying very hard to remember something which has not yet taken place”. Lee offers genuinely transporting literary criticism, unearthing the elegance and complexity of the work, but admits the compulsive production of a book a year diluted the impact and sometimes the quality. Still, she singles out three – Family and Friends, Latecomers and The Next Big Thing – as truly “outstanding” novels. Thankfully, it is no longer cool to Brookner-bash. This astute and tireless biography succeeds, against the odds, in unearthing the author – who would be appalled by our scrutiny. Above all, it shows that the work deserves our full attention.

entries.title: Under Story by Chloe Benjamin review – this time-reversal melodrama is quantum hokum
entries.summary: A grieving couple who have lost their son find a way to a mirror universe where time runs backwards – but the narrative machinery is shonky and distractingThere is something farcical – grotesque, even – about life played in reverse. A child falling into a tree. A sandwich emerging from a mouth, bite by reconstituted bite. A doctor unstitching a wound. The world is strange in any order, but rewind
entries.content:
There is something farcical – grotesque, even – about life played in reverse. A child falling into a tree. A sandwich emerging from a mouth, bite by reconstituted bite. A doctor unstitching a wound. The world is strange in any order, but rewind helps us notice – makes the ordinary absurd.

Novels that pick a fight with forward momentum tend to harness this absurdity, revel in it. In The Cockroach (2019), Ian McEwan gives us a sneering Brexit fable about political nostalgia. If voters want to turn back the clock, let them. He unleashes “Economic Reversalism”, which sees employees pay for the privilege of work, and every pound sent back to where it came from. In Time’s Arrow (1991), Martin Amis inverts the Holocaust. Just imagine it, he dares us: a network of sanatoriums instead of death camps. A vast machinery of reparation run by benevolent Nazis. How monstrously laughable.

Joining this backwards bunch is Chloe Benjamin with her third novel, Under Story. It conjures a universe that mirrors our own (a “duoverse”), populated by doppelgangers; a place where the past might be undone, because it hasn’t happened yet.

Here are the fictional facts. In the duoverse, ordinary human life begins underground. Mycelium grow a corpse from rot, like a 3D printer for gizzards. A heart starts beating, for reasons, and a fully grown human crawls up from the soil riddled with elderly ailments, but with a box-fresh brain. Once they’re cleaned up and DNA profiled – the work of “overtakers” – these new/old people are delivered to their children, but in the postal, rather than the obstetric, sense. The doorbell rings.

Brains grow older; bodies grow younger. Cancers unbloom. Cataracts fade. Children raise their parents until they’re spry enough to cope on their own. Nursing homes are convalescent kindergartens. And down at the other end of life, kindergartens are dementia clinics full of geriatric toddlers. Death is birth: neonates are shoved up their mothers in maternity morgues, swallowed by the amniotic dark.

It’s ghoulish stuff, body horror territory: wards of women surgically forced to eat their babies with their hungry vaginas. You might expect – even hope for – some literary depravity: Benjamin Button reimagined by William Burroughs or Agustina Bazterrica. But Under Story is a love story. We follow a forward-born couple, Laurel and Eli, who are grieving their son, Silas. Could a round trip to the duoverse summon him back? Might it also help them to forgive one another? What follows is a 500-page melodrama of parental devotion and quantum hokum. Imagine Orpheus and Eurydice meets Interstellar, but starring Tom Hanks from Big.

Using a combination of speculative physics and prophetic dreams, Laurel and Eli find their way to a portal under the ice of Antarctica and into the duoverse. They adjust quickly to its topsy-turvy logic: September follows October, Obama follows Trump, and the analogue revolution is under way (the record player has just been invented). Handily, the climate is also unravaging – extinct species popping up from the ground like the mushrooms that remade them.

The key to it all is entropy: “this universe moves toward the Big Bang, and entropy is reversed,” Eli explains. He’s a physicist; Laurel is a mycologist. They’ll both do a great deal of explaining.

There can be no life without entropy, but that’s not the problem here. Plenty of imagined worlds are nonsense, and gloriously so. The problem is that Benjamin keeps drawing our attention to her shonky narrative machinery. She answers questions we’d never thought to ask. We learn that “Christmas exists here, even though Jesus won’t be born for two thousand years” and that reverse folks can’t choose to procreate, because the decision is already waiting for them when they grovel out of the placental dirt.

Benjamin’s last novel, 2018’s The Immortalists, was also about foretold lives: four siblings who learn the dates of their deaths from a fortune teller. But the point – and lure – of that novel was doubt. Was the prophecy real or self-fulfilling? Is there a difference? Benjamin left those questions with us. In Under Story, she seems unsure her cosmic premise can carry its own mysteries. But the more we learn, the more distracted we are. And that’s before Benjamin busts out some last-act theatrics – mystical anagrams and fortuitous gadgetry – or subjects us to a death-birth. It’s hard to trust a novel that doesn’t trust itself.

Part of the problem is length. Rewound life is a gimmick, a thought experiment. The books that do it best are wry, incisive and short (the anticlockwise archetype, F Scott Fitzgerald’s The Curious Case of Benjamin Button, is a fleet 40-page story). The longer Laurel and Eli stay in the duoverse, the more contrived it all feels, because the more contrived it has to be. It’s hard to live backwards with dignity, and Benjamin knows it. And so she picks and chooses which bodily functions work in which direction. People walk and talk normally. Have conceptionless sex. Breathe and eat and excrete. It’s entropy galore, except for the life cycle. The author has her backwards cake, and eats it too.

But there are much easier ways to meddle with the past and its sorrows (see Scott Alexander Howard’s The Other Valley or Aja Gabel’s Lightbreakers), which makes all of Benjamin’s picking and choosing feel particularly gruesome. Her duoverse has been elaborately rigged to produce a scene of filial reunion. She has violated the laws of physics, reanimated the dead and turned women’s bodies into tombs all in order to weaponise parental grief.

It’s meant to make us weep, to rouse mighty questions about ageless love, free will and our intimate connection to the planet. But here are some of the questions I scribbled in the margins of Under Story: if every fossil is a future creature, are palaeontologists dino-killers? Will the suffragettes fight to relinquish the vote? If vaginas work backwards, are penises the same: meaty little vacuum cleaners, hoovering up sperm? Once you’ve written a line like that you know your suspension of disbelief has well and truly snapped. And maybe something else has too.

entries.title: Switzy by Emma Cline review – this Booker-listed account of a man’s last days is profoundly moving
entries.summary: Struggling with Alzheimer’s, the central character sets out on his final journey to a euthanasia clinicThe word “Alzheimer’s” never appears in Switzy, Emma Cline’s third novel, which arrives pre-endorsed as a Booker prize longlistee. But we can be certain that it is the disease afflicting its central character, David Hastings – certain in a way he finds it increasingly hard to be about anything.Wh
entries.content:
The word “Alzheimer’s” never appears in Switzy, Emma Cline’s third novel, which arrives pre-endorsed as a Booker prize longlistee. But we can be certain that it is the disease afflicting its central character, David Hastings – certain in a way he finds it increasingly hard to be about anything.

When the novel begins, David and his assistant Cody are aboard a private jet flying from his home in the US to the UK. Landing at London City airport (which the book, experiencing its own senior moment, situates in the countryside), they visit David’s daughter and her family before travelling on to Zurich (hence “Switzy”). One more appointment, a catchup with an old boarding school roommate called Tom, awaits just over the French border, after which David will be euthanised at a facility resembling Dignitas.

David is wealthy. Not wealthy enough to own the jet he’s flying around in – that’s a loan from his boss – but someone to whom its polished doors, “that slid silently and obligingly out of sight”, are of a piece with the comfortable, largely frictionless world through which he moves. He has had a career in business, chief financial officer of some undefined entity – one large enough for a forensic accounting firm to be required when it became apparent David, in an early sign of the seriousness of his impairment, had mistakenly scattered its money into “an archipelago of overseas accounts”.

For all the capital he has accumulated, David has been “a support person, a man whose name would never be known”, who sat at a desk and “made certain numbers swell up and other numbers recede”. Has it been a happy life? Well, the revelation or otherwise of that is one of the strands running through this extraordinarily well-made novel.

How ill is David? Not so ill as to disqualify him from choosing euthanasia, but enough that navigating the world, from finding his hotel room to operating a phone, holding up his end of a conversation or understanding how and why he has offended someone, has become deeply problematic. He has reached the stage of his illness where, we learn from references to past events, he has woken up in his car uncertain of how he came to be there, soiled himself, upset employees, even lost the ability to tie his shoelaces. Sometimes he forgets he has eaten until a burp, tasting of lunch, reminds him of the fact. At other times he experiences the feeling “of coming into a room and the room offering no answers as to why he was there”. His world is full of aftermath but often frustratingly empty of cause.

He compares his situation to that of a “mental ice floe, populated only by David, floating off into the polar darkness”. The text elegantly reflects this, its atomised paragraphs separated by white space – treacherous voids across which the thread of David’s awareness might not stretch from one moment to another. Yet as his comprehension thins, our own deepens. As his self-referential and fragmented stream of consciousness, often rich in similes, rebounds between the inputs of wherever he happens to be – in a car, at a restaurant, walking the streets of one city or another, always with Cody beside him – and his piecemeal memories, we begin to catch the resonances he no longer can.

I think it is probably impossible to remain unmoved by David’s journey towards death, but as I accompanied him on it, I registered a nagging doubt that became increasingly insistent. David’s condition is worsening; he knows the day is coming when “he’d find that the contents of his brain had been excised with an ice-cream scooper instead of these dainty little teaspoons, here and there”. But in the case of the storyline involving Tom, David’s faltering memory just so happens to fall into precisely the pattern of revelation employed by a traditional trauma-plot novel.

Characters in such books, as the critic Parul Sehgal noted in her 2021 New Yorker essay on the subject, “work to fill in the gaps of partial, haunting recollections”. Throughout Switzy, clues bob to the surface of David’s consciousness about some shameful event that soured things between himself and Tom at boarding school in the 1960s. One involves Tom’s sister “narrowing her eyes at him across the lawn at graduation”. No further context for the look is provided, for us or David, but as soon as it was mentioned I felt confident that the closer the meeting with Tom came, the more would be revealed about their shared past.

This certainty that novelistic convention would be obeyed works against the uncertainty Cline otherwise evokes so brilliantly. It’s true that with Alzheimer’s long-term memories can persist as short-term memories cease to imprint. But David, too, appears to be searching for precisely what happened between himself and Tom. The memory is conveniently unavailable, provoking suspense, and then, just as conveniently, it returns to provide satisfaction. The reader’s knowledge that David will remember – an expectation drummed into us from myriad stories that work this way – runs counter to the reality of his predicament, to which neither narrative nor real-world logic applies. Behind his chaotic decline, the “unknowable soup” of his reality in which cause and effect have become terrifyingly uncoupled, hums a perfectly calibrated narrative machine as smooth and obliging in its operation as the doors of his private jet.

When the novel moves past the Tom storyline, as it does with about 50 pages to go, it becomes its best self. Untethered from the duties of revelation it can fully immerse us in David’s pocked reality: impressionistic, arresting, upsetting, even funny. Earlier in the book, when reflecting on losing the name for the plastic cap on a shoelace (an aglet), he thinks that that one “was probably okay. Sure, toss it overboard.” By contrast – although it’s tempting fate to say it – the last pages of Switzy, which mingle horror, beauty, absurdity, and a sense of profound finality, will probably stay with me for ever.

entries.title: The Future Starts With Us by Gordon Brown review – the ex-PM’s recipe for beating populism
entries.summary: Global crises are tightly linked to how we treat each other at the local level, argues this optimistic book In times of crisis, there is one person to whom the left still turns for guidance.More than a decade and a half after leaving government, Gordon Brown has mellowed into the Labour party’s favourite wise elder; one who has never disappointed the faithful by going off to make a ton of money, r
entries.content:
In times of crisis, there is one person to whom the left still turns for guidance.

More than a decade and a half after leaving government, Gordon Brown has mellowed into the Labour party’s favourite wise elder; one who has never disappointed the faithful by going off to make a ton of money, remaining quietly committed to public service and deeply engaged with the world’s knottier problems. Having successfully led the global response to the financial crash of 2008, and advocated powerfully during the pandemic for global cooperation against the virus, he was never going to simply sit back and shrug as the world spiralled into conflict and chaos under Donald Trump.

But still, I thought, as I opened his latest book on the collapse of the old world order, it’s barely three years since his last tome on fixing the general mess (Permacrisis, written with the economists Mohammed El-Erian and Michael Spence). Does he really have anything new to say, or is this prolific output born mostly out of frustration that the world has seemingly stopped listening?

A bit of both, it turns out. The new twist involves some polling commissioned to back Brown’s hunch that deep down voters actually crave a return to the more stable, orderly, benevolent world of the 2000s, despite voting repeatedly for the opposite. But to reach this research, readers must first wade through multiple chapters ramming home once again what’s wrong with the world, which will have many readers nodding in agreement without telling them much they didn’t already know. What could have been a deep, rich essay thus becomes a book: essentially a sermon on the moral failings of neoliberalism, ending in a rousing hymn to hope, echoing both the rhythm of his best party conference speeches and the broad themes of Andy Burnham’s first few weeks in power. (So much so, indeed, that you wonder how much the two men have been talking lately.)

What is new for Brown, however, is that this book is preoccupied less with economics than with the argument that collapsing civic ties – the fact that we’re less likely now than a generation ago to be part of a club, trade union, church or community group – have helped undermine “the very idea that we are all in this together, that there are common causes worth fighting for”.

What could be just another nostalgic, even reactionary, argument for a bygone age when everyone knew their neighbours is tempered by Brown’s willingness to acknowledge that much of this togetherness was built on the unpaid labour of women stuck at home. But it’s also brought up to date by his argument that this fraying of social bonds – especially in towns fallen on hard times, now leaning towards populist politicians – is actively connected to fragmentation and the retreat from multilateralism on the world stage. It’s time, he argues, to stop treating breakdown at home and breakup abroad as separate phenomena.

Beating populism obviously means tackling the economic grievances – the disappearing jobs and hollowed-out high streets – on which it feeds in post-industrial communities across the US and Europe. Yet the general rolling chaos that populists tend to unleash on the world stage makes it actively harder for everyone else to build stable and prosperous economies, creating a vicious circle of decline.

Brown’s answer is to build a virtuous circle instead, from the ground up. Strengthening civic ties should make people feel less lonely, more secure and trusting, and thus hopefully more relaxed about their governments acting generously and collaboratively at an international level. That, of course, is key to tackling everything from the climate crisis, to global poverty, to forming the kind of alliances with other middle-ranking powers that might prevent a country like the UK being totally steamrollered in a standoff between the US and China. At least, that’s the theory.

The idea that dying high streets at home and rogue superpowers overseas are different threads of the same great unravelling does at least create a clear narrative hook on which a new Labour prime minister can hang lots of otherwise seemingly disparate ideas, and seek political buy-in for them both in the “red wall” and among big-city liberals. There’s material here too for a foreign secretary capable – as Ed Miliband arguably is – of thinking big and acting local, connecting foreign policy much more closely to progress at home. But just how plausible is it?

Enter the new polling, of 32,000 people across 20 developed countries, from Argentina to the UK to South Korea. It distinguishes between “zero sum” thinkers – people who believe they can only win if others lose, colouring their attitudes to everything from trade to immigration – and a more generous “civic core”, open to some compromise for the greater good, on whom progressive governments depend. In the UK, at least, the latter group still outweighs the former, with a significant group lying between the two that Brown reckons could be persuaded to heed the better angels of their natures.

He then calculates the impact of measures like reducing economic grievances, or increasing people’s face-to-face interaction with others from different religious or racial backgrounds, on propensity to vote for populists. To cut a long story short: deploy all the virtuous circle measures together, and with luck (and time), you might have a potent means of tackling populism from the ground up.

Rather less convincing, however, is his formula for restoring the international rules-based order, starting with a new universal charter to which responsible countries could sign up. We already have plenty of grand statements of intent and bodies to enforce them, from the international criminal court to the Paris climate change accords: what’s missing is governments prepared to actually stick to the rules.

Unusually for Brown, the best of this book isn’t in the big-picture thinking on globalisation or the rise of China, but in lessons learned at neighbourhood level. After a life spent trying to push through huge decisions, he writes, only recently has he begun thinking that he should have started small.

One obvious hurdle is that the neighbourly civic engagement he favours is of the decidedly muscular, worthy kind. The clubs Brown sees as capable of teaching “active citizenship” are those that demand the most time and effort from volunteers – and they have died out. Just signing up for fun times doesn’t count. Like the good son of the manse he is, Brown personally practises what he preaches in Kirkcaldy, where he is heavily engaged with local charities. I’m not sure your average Briton, spending their downtime from work scrolling exhaustedly on the sofa, will feel the same.

Then again Brown does say that cynicism like mine is part of the problem; that if liberal politics is to compete with demagogues, it can’t simply confine itself to the art of the possible – it must “show it can make the desirable possible”. Even if, just occasionally, that sounds like wishful thinking.

entries.title: ‘Who would dare take on Elizabeth Jane Howard’s fans?’ Louisa Young on reviving the Cazalet Chronicles
entries.summary: The author’s new trilogy continues her aunt’s beloved family saga. What would happen next to the sprawling cast of characters ... and could she pull it off? In the late 1980s Elizabeth Jane Howard was wondering what to write next. Jane, as she was always known, was at that time the author of seven novels. Her debut, The Beautiful Visit, had won the John Llewellyn Rhys prize in 1951 when she was 28
entries.content:
In the late 1980s Elizabeth Jane Howard was wondering what to write next. Jane, as she was always known, was at that time the author of seven novels. Her debut, The Beautiful Visit, had won the John Llewellyn Rhys prize in 1951 when she was 28 years old and The Long View (1956) was one of the first novels written with reverse chronology. Her talent was somewhat overshadowed in a tawdry world by her drop-dead beauty and by her having briefly been an actor (and by the famous lovers and husbands she walked out on, including Sir Peter Scott, the ornithologist and conservationist, in 1946, and Kingsley Amis, who was then himself a famous novelist, in 1983).

Stuck, she asked her stepson Martin Amis which of two projects she should go for: an updated version of Sense and Sensibility, or a family saga based on her own life? He said, do the family saga. Jane’s family project developed into the Cazalet Chronicles: five volumes in which she fictionalised her life’s experience, divided between three young female cousins, Polly, Clary and Louise, and a cast of 52 more named characters, set between London and a grandparental family home in Sussex.

The first volume, The Light Years (1990), opens in 1937, and the series closes in 1958. From a slow beginning, the Cazalets grew into a worldwide phenomenon, selling millions of copies, and has been in print ever since.

As each one came out I tore through them: not just because Jane was brilliant and I was a fan, but also because she was my aunt. My grandmother, the sculptor Kathleen Scott, had been Jane’s mother-in-law: mother of Peter Scott and of my father Wayland Young. In 1990 I was writing a biography of Kathleen – so Jane was a living witness for me. It put my smoky-voiced, glamorous aunt and me in a peculiar overlap: she, in her 60s, was writing a fictional version of the actual life she had lived, and I, at 29, was writing a putatively factual version of the same things, though they had happened before I was born.

That was my first book; the last Cazalet novel was to be Jane’s last. I was so ready to sit at her feet, listen to her stories, to “carry her reticule”, as she put it, when she went to literary festivals. In her beautiful house in Bungay, Suffolk, where she lived with her brother Colin, known as Monkey, we talked about everything. How funny life is, how circular! We gossiped about people I’d never met, from decades before my birth. Jane gave me one version; Monkey gave me another. She loved me, I think, at least initially, for my dad’s sake, and because I was a young woman, becoming a writer.

Through the mirrors and veils of her fiction, I recognised people and situations, saw hints of truth about my own family’s mysteries. In reality, Kathleen Scott and 19-year-old Jane had not got on at all – it was a hurried and frightened wartime marriage, a failure immediately. In the Cazalet books, Kathleen is fictionalised as Zee and comes across as an absolute monster, who threatened to kill Jane/Louise.

But my father adored his mother: “She was always saying she was going to kill people!” he said. “It was a turn of phrase … but the wrong one for Jane then.” My own mother had been secretary to Peter (fictionalised as Michael Hadleigh), and had lent the penniless Jane money to leave him. Both the real people and the characters in the books, only in their twenties, overlapped during and after the war in west London, where I lived. The past seemed so close, and so far away. And of course it’s always fascinating to think of your parents’ generation being young, and messy.

I read the volumes avidly as they came out, and ran back to her wanting to ask, “Jane, is that real? Was that true?” But these can be hard questions, and impertinent. Fiction is meant to be emotionally true, not factually. “True in spirit,” she told me. At the same time as she protected her own version, she wanted to protect those she loved. This curious palimpsest gives the fiction an astonishing extra tension, as those who have read her memoir, Slipstream (2002), or the biography by Artemis Cooper (A Dangerous Innocence, 2016) can testify.

The Cazalet Chronicles are often described as a comfort read, both because they contain servants and food and clothes, and because they provide such a deeply complete fictional world for escaping into from an unsatisfactory real one. But being upper-middle-class doesn’t protect the characters from rape, child abuse, incest, abandonment, suicide, divorce, concentration camps, war, fear, loss, cancer or death. They are sometimes seen as somehow lighter than her earlier, more literary works, but she didn’t think they were, and they’re not: I’ve read them many times now and each time they get darker. Their surge of popularity during Covid makes perfect sense to me: the characters, like the rest of us during the lockdowns, were restricted by events beyond their control. They couldn’t go where they wanted; they couldn’t be with who they wanted to be with, they were constrained and scared and bored. And, in the main, they survived. Which is always reassuring.

When something works, we want more of it. I always wanted more Cazalets. Chronicles should go on. But it never crossed my mind to imagine I could pick up Jane’s mantle. Until it did – which was as a PS in a “What Next?” email of my own to my agent. I was suggesting a long list of bad ideas, and then at the end: “Or I could always try to continue the Cazalet Chronicles”. It was a joke! Jane was a great writer. Who would dare face the ranks of devotees, still so dedicated and protective? Or launch into the continuity perils of 500,000 words?

I realised it wasn’t such a terrible idea when Jane’s daughter, my cousin, gave her blessing. I found a message from Jane telling me a novel of mine was “a triumph”. My agent was all for it. We went to Jane’s own publishers, and worked with some of her editors. There would be three volumes, we decided. One would just be silly – why wake everybody up for that? – and more than three was too far ahead to see.

I read the books again, thinking about how I would do it. Loose ends trailed before me, begging to be picked up. Pitfalls beckoned. The unsettling incestuous romance between half-siblings Juliet and Neville needed closure. Villy, Louise’s mother, was a victim of being a 20th-century woman as well as being a bad mother. Mainly because she had to have all her teeth out, I wanted her to have a better ending than just being dumped and her four children disliking her. Virtuous, kind Rachel, who for years didn’t even realise she was a lesbian, deserved better too (I am regularly accosted by young gay women wanting to know what I have planned for her, because it had better be good). And then there is the great unresolved issue of Louise’s abandoned son, Sebastian, who was too close to home in reality for Jane to address in fiction. And look, there’s my fictionalised grandparents, Zee and The Judge; there’s fictionalised Dad, here called Hugo, disguised as a cousin for propriety’s sake. It was these novels that told me how much Jane had loved Dad. Alas, she had him die in the War, and this is not the kind of saga where he can come back to life played by a different actor. (In reality he had six children and a sixty-year marriage, and lived till 2009.)

It did seem to me that the characters were all still there, their lives continuing, just off-stage. The fifth Cazalet book, All Change, ends at Christmas 1958. I was born three months later. I was there! The idea that their lives might be up to me and my imagination was intoxicating, trepidation-inducing and inspiring. It’s not about inventing things to happen to them: they are already in full flow. I am chasing after them with a notebook. I make it seamless for the reader by continuing Jane’s elegant structure of tessellated sections, each from one person’s point of view, but I do allow the way I write, my generation’s use of language, to bring things forward in time, as time itself moves forward.

I’m now the age Jane was when she was writing this fictionalised account of her life. Can these three novels count as mine, when I’ve broken into her world to write them? I’m not sure that’s answerable. But equally, what a circle it is, from writing about the young girl Jane in my biography of my grandmother, to the picking up of her baton now, after her death, beyond her knowledge. By bringing these characters on, of necessity I make them mine. Because this isn’t a pastiche, an imitation, or a homage. It’s a living story. The family chronicle rolls on through time in reality as it does on the page. I might even put it in a book …

entries.title: Could this policy fix the care system and slash student debt at the same time?

entries.content:
The UK’s social care sector is in crisis. Costs are spiralling, with many local councils forced to dedicate the vast majority of their budgets to it. At the same time, more and more families are seeing their savings disappear into the black hole of nursing home fees. With an ageing population, the problem is set to get worse.

In only his second week as prime minister, Andy Burnham pledged to succeed where so many of his predecessors have failed: by fixing Britain’s social care system. And yet, as parliament returns from recess, the new-ish administration is still worryingly unclear about how it will do this. Despite Burnham declaring that care workers should enjoy better compensation, we don’t know how he plans to pay for any of it – not least because he has kept Starmer’s campaign pledge to not raise income tax, VAT or national insurance. At the moment, it looks as though it will be impossible to square the circle.

What the government needs is big, innovative ideas. We should look to history for inspiration, while also absorbing the lessons of past mistakes.

How about national service – but instead of entering the military, recruits are pledged to the NHS? Eye-catching, but ultimately not right, at least not in that form. Forcing young people to do work they’d prefer not to, when there isn’t even an enemy at the gates, will only lead to bad results. Indeed, the army has already learned this: compulsory recruits in the postwar period were typically unmotivated and incompetent; a drag rather than a boost to the military’s performance.

But that’s a crude precedent. We can take more relevant inspiration from elsewhere. For example, young men in Austria who do not wish to serve in the military can instead opt for health or social care work; many end up driving ambulances. The trade-off is that they do nine months instead of six. In Norway, conscientious objectors were, until 2012, able to perform “civilian national service”, working in community settings such as primary schools or nursing homes, and accruing points towards university entry for doing so.

Thinking along similar lines, how about this? The government offers recent school leavers a deal: 50% off their total university fees if they first spend a year volunteering in social care. (You could even up the ante: 100% off if they commit to two years; full back pay with a bonus if they stay in the profession.)

There are many reasons to take this proposal seriously. First, it is not just social care that is in crisis. University funding is, too. Right now, UK universities are panicking because student enrolment fees no longer keep them in the black. But at the same time, undergraduates are being presented with eye-watering loan bills and interest rates at levels that make capital repayment much harder. We are rapidly approaching a cliff edge. The government is going to have to fix the system one way or the other. Why not do something innovative and radical at the same time?

The overall maths might work surprisingly well. If uptake is sufficiently high, the state gets an enormous amount of free (in the short term) labour to offset the costs of lost loan revenue. If that sounds exploitative, remember that it would be in the interests of young people themselves (in the longer term) because they would leave university with a heck of a lot less debt.

But the upsides go beyond just money. At the moment, unscrupulous agencies too often rely on low-paid migrant labour, ignoring the linguistic and caring skills required do a safe and competent job. A scheme like this would open up a new pool for recruitment – of eager-to-learn young people at the start of their careers.

Of course, they would have to undergo proper training and would only get the discount if they complete the programme to a certified high level. Along the way, some would discover that care work can be deeply rewarding; that the current stigmatisation of this kind of employment just doesn’t tally with reality.

I know, because since I broke my neck in a rock-climbing accident in 2023, I have relied on 24-hour live-in care. I am lucky to be with a very good agency, which only employs highly competent and conscientious staff (from all over the world). I have seen up close just how rewarding and dignified care work can be. Sure, there are some icky parts to looking after a man who can’t go to the toilet by himself. But all my care workers take real pride in helping me live as close to a normal life as possible. Of course, they’re not on footballers’ wages. But they get a very visible amount of life satisfaction from helping me find mine.

One of the most interesting care workers I’ve met was covering holiday earlier in the summer. Originally from Ireland, she had just finished a two-year master’s degree at King’s College London (by coincidence where I teach, in a different department). She is now a qualified dietitian, who in future will be working in hospitals. But until she makes that transition she is spending a year with my spinal agency, after having been employed as a care worker in Ireland for two years prior to her degree. It’s a job she finds deeply rewarding.

I am confident that if we incentivised UK students to try social care before university, many would consider rejoining once they had graduated. This would help to reduce wider stigma around care work as the preserve of poor, often vulnerable migrant workers, assumed to be doing it only because no one else will.

Look, I’m neither a government accountant nor a policy expert. Perhaps when we’ve crunched the numbers, it just doesn’t work. But from where I’m sitting this has the potential to be a win-win of the sort that could define the Burnham administration. All the scheme needs is a name, and there’s an obvious one for the taking: “Care First”.

Dr Paul Sagar is a reader in political theory at King’s College London.

Further reading

Labours of Love: The Crisis of Care by Madeleine Bunting (Granta, £9.99)

The Courage to Care: Nurses, Families and Hope by Christie Watson (Vintage, £10.99)

Who Cares by Emily Kenway (Headline, £12.99)
